expect.statement: Head-to-head randomized evidence on antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis, as identified by a systematic review and network meta-analysis with searches to June 2020 and by two other systematic reviews that contain the same trials (searches to November 2018: five of the six; to March 2026: all six), consists of six small, short (21 to 42 days), single-site trials with 395 participants in Thailand, Iran and China, mostly inpatients and mostly men, each comparing two of six antipsychotics (aripiprazole, haloperidol, olanzapine, paliperidone extended-release, quetiapine, risperidone); none had a placebo or no-medication arm, and two are titled as trials in amphetamine psychosis. The network meta-analysis reports that each trial found no significant difference between its two drugs on the main psychotic symptoms (the 2026 review instead gives one aripiprazole–risperidone trial a between-group p < 0.001 on positive symptoms, and the 2019 review describes that trial in both directions), and the trials were too small to show that the drugs work equally well. Chaining the trials through their shared drugs, the network meta-analysis estimated lower symptom scores at the end of treatment on olanzapine (standardized mean difference −1.09, 95% CI −1.89 to −0.28) and quetiapine (−0.86, −1.61 to −0.11) than on risperidone, and higher scores on aripiprazole than on four of the other drugs (the review compared end-of-treatment scores, not changes from baseline); these are indirect estimates only, rated low certainty by the authors because data came partly from open-label trials and the trials differ in participants and design, and both advantages over risperidone rest on one open-label trial of haloperidol against risperidone with 44 participants. Dropout did not differ, but its intervals were too wide to be informative. Because none of these trials had a placebo arm, they cannot show whether antipsychotics speed recovery beyond what abstinence alone achieves; symptoms fell steeply in every arm, but the large effect sizes the other two reviews report (d = 3.4 to 5.5 in the 4-week trials) are changes from baseline within each arm, which cannot separate a drug effect from recovery with abstinence and time. Two small placebo-controlled trials, which the network meta-analysis did not include, enrolled people whose symptoms had already largely settled: aripiprazole for 8 weeks in 37 outpatients (symptoms fell more than on placebo, between-group p = 0.032) and paliperidone extended-release for 12 weeks in 80 people stabilized on drug-treatment wards before discharge (reported as favouring paliperidone, p = 0.006; 28% against 55% lost to follow-up); they bear on continued treatment after the acute episode rather than on its treatment. The only trial against usual care (Hong Kong, 2026; 165 people with stimulant-induced psychosis, about nine in ten of whom had used methamphetamine, mostly mildly ill) randomized them to aripiprazole, paliperidone or usual care, in which 55% were antipsychotic-free at randomization and 24% at 24 months. On clinicians' global severity ratings (CGI-S), aripiprazole improved more than usual care at 12 months (−0.55 points, 95% CI −1.03 to −0.07; d −0.31) and at 24 months, when ratings were no longer blind; paliperidone did not differ; and symptom ratings (BPRS-24) showed no consistent difference. That trial's registered primary outcome, relapse over 36 months, was changed after the trial ended, first to the BPRS-24 and then to the global ratings it reports; 17% of its participants had an earlier diagnosis of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, which the registry lists as an exclusion, and without them the 12-month CGI-S difference was not significant (p = 0.12); only 54% were assessed at 24 months. No trial has followed people after the antipsychotic was stopped, so how long to treat and the risk of relapse after stopping are unstudied. Side effects were not pooled; as the 2026 review tabulates them, extrapyramidal symptoms occurred in 15 of 29 participants on haloperidol and none of 29 on olanzapine in the olanzapine–haloperidol trial (probably the single trial of the 2009 Cochrane review that narrative reviews describe), 10 against 2 stopped early, and in one aripiprazole–risperidone trial 7 of 21 on aripiprazole and none of 21 on risperidone stopped because of adverse effects; in the usual-care trial, serious adverse events were one suicide in the aripiprazole arm and three paliperidone discontinuations (atrial fibrillation, QTc prolongation, acute renal failure with pneumonia). Two narrative reviews state that acute psychosis usually resolves with abstinence alone, citing early studies of amphetamine psychosis published between 1958 and 1980 or an online clinical reference entry. How often psychosis persists after stopping is described in section 9.
expect.magnitude: Six head-to-head randomized trials (searches to June 2020), 395 participants, 42 to 120 per trial, 21 to 42 days; no placebo arm. Network estimates against risperidone, main symptoms at the end of treatment (SMD of final values, not of change scores): olanzapine −1.09 (−1.89 to −0.28) and quetiapine −0.86 (−1.61 to −0.11), indirect only; haloperidol −0.60 (−1.20 to 0.01), paliperidone extended-release −0.33 (−0.69 to 0.03) and aripiprazole 0.27 (−0.13 to 0.68), direct. Aripiprazole against olanzapine 1.36 (0.46 to 2.26), quetiapine 1.13 (0.28 to 1.98), haloperidol 0.87 (0.14 to 1.60) and paliperidone extended-release 0.60 (0.06 to 1.14), indirect. No direct comparison significant. Dropout odds ratios against risperidone 0.18 to 2.77, every interval including 1. Authors' GRADE: low or very low for every estimate. Two further systematic reviews share these trials (searches to November 2018: 6 trials, 314 participants; to March 2026: 8 trials, 514 participants) and add two placebo-controlled trials after the acute episode: aripiprazole, 8 weeks, 37 participants, between-group p = 0.032; paliperidone extended-release, 12 weeks, 80 participants, p = 0.006, lost to follow-up 28% vs 55% (OR 0.31, 0.12 to 0.79). Within-arm changes from baseline in the 4-week trials d = 3.4 to 5.5 (not treatment effects). Usual-care trial (165 participants, 24 months): CGI-S change against usual care at 12 months aripiprazole −0.55 (−1.03 to −0.07), d −0.31, paliperidone −0.40 (−0.86 to 0.06); at 24 months, unblinded, −0.65 (−1.22 to −0.09) and −0.02 (−0.60 to 0.56); BPRS-24 no consistent difference; 70% assessed at 12 months, 54% at 24 months; registered primary outcome (relapse over 36 months) not reported. Side effects, trial level as tabulated by the 2026 review: extrapyramidal symptoms 15 of 29 on haloperidol vs 0 of 29 on olanzapine (OR 63.07, 3.52 to 1129.74); discontinuation for adverse effects 7 of 21 on aripiprazole vs 0 of 21 on risperidone (OR 22.24, 1.18 to 420.39).
expect.grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence, read through three systematic reviews that share their trials (Srisurapanont et al., 2021, a network meta-analysis, AMSTAR 2 low confidence; Fluyau et al., 2019, critically low; Hall et al., 2026, low) and one trial against usual care read in full together with its registry record (Chung et al., 2026; RoB 2 high); the eight shorter trial reports themselves have not been read. Starts high. Risk of bias −1: two of the six head-to-head trials were open-label and allocation concealment was unclear in four; both indirect advantages over risperidone, and three of the four against aripiprazole, are chained through the open-label haloperidol–risperidone pilot trial (44 participants); the two placebo-controlled trials are known only through reviews that describe their analyses inconsistently; and the usual-care trial changed its primary outcome after the data were collected, lost 30% of assessments at 12 months and 46% at 24 months, and rated its second year unblinded. Taken alone, the comparison with usual care would be rated down two levels for risk of bias; certainty would be very low either way. Indirectness −1: the network is a chain without a closed loop, so every indirect estimate rests on transitivity, which the authors themselves doubt (participants and designs differ); two trials are titled as amphetamine psychosis; the placebo-controlled trials enrolled people whose symptoms had largely settled; the usual-care trial included cocaine-induced psychosis and 17% with an earlier schizophrenia or schizoaffective diagnosis, and its usual care included antipsychotics for most participants by 24 months. No trial compares an antipsychotic with none during an acute episode, the claim's open question. Imprecision −2: 37 to 120 participants per short trial, every direct head-to-head interval includes no difference, dropout odds ratios have intervals as wide as 0.00 to 218, and the usual-care trial's 12-month CGI-S difference (−0.55, −1.03 to −0.07) comes from 116 people assessed. Inconsistency not downgraded, though it can hardly be judged: the network's global I² of 0% for main symptoms rests on one degree of freedom (six two-arm trials of six drugs, no closed loop), contributed by the two aripiprazole–risperidone trials; the three reviews read one aripiprazole–risperidone trial (Farnia et al., 2014) in different directions; and in the usual-care trial the global ratings and the symptom ratings disagree. Publication bias not assessable with so few trials; not downgraded, noted. Very low. The network estimates are differences in end-of-treatment scores (the review used final values for all symptom analyses), not in how much symptoms fell. Status mixed (changed from single study, which rested on there being one network meta-analysis): the three reviews share their trials and count once (METHODS §6.3), but the claim now also rests on three trials against placebo or usual care from three independent groups (Malaysia, China, Hong Kong). The head-to-head trials test five different drug pairs and their directions are reported inconsistently across the reviews; the trials against placebo or usual care favour the antipsychotic on some outcomes but not on others (the usual-care trial's symptom ratings; paliperidone at 24 months), in different populations and with serious flaws, and no explanation has been tested. Counting direction alone, the three trials against placebo or usual care would meet the definition of replicated; this reader judges mixed the more accurate label because their populations, outcomes and risk of bias differ. The two Chinese head-to-head trials share authors, and the narrative reviews describe some of the same trials. The olanzapine–haloperidol trial (Leelahanaj et al., 2005), probably the trial the narrative reviews describe as the 2009 Cochrane review's single trial with 58 participants, is listed with 58 (29 and 29) by the 2019 and 2026 reviews and with 56 (29 and 27) by the network meta-analysis. The placebo-controlled aripiprazole trial (Sulaiman et al., 2013) may have randomized people after an open-label aripiprazole phase reported in a dissertation (Sulaiman, 2011): that phase's end PANSS (51.6) equals the trial's entry PANSS in the network meta-analysis (editors' inference; the trial report has not been read).
expect.evidence.20.extracted: Registered primary outcome before enrolment (version 7) and until July 2025 (version 13): the relative risk of psychosis relapse over 36 months. After primary completion (31 May 2024) it was changed to the BPRS-24 at 12 and 24 months (version 14) and then to the CGI scales at 12 and 24 months (version 15), the outcome the article reports as primary; relapse is not reported in the article. The registry lists a diagnosis of schizophrenia as an exclusion criterion.
expect.plain: Three reviews found eight small, short trials of medicines for meth psychosis, about 500 people in all. Six compared one medicine with another and found no clear winner. Two small trials against a dummy pill, in people already improving, and one two-year trial against usual care favoured the medicine on some measures, but these trials have serious flaws. Nobody has studied stopping the medicine.

grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Aripiprazole–risperidone trials without a consistent direction; paliperidone better than placebo after the acute phase but not than usual care; global and symptom ratings disagree in the usual-care trial; no explanation tested (status mixed). Certainty already at its floor.

expect.statement: In a systematic review of studies of methamphetamine-associated psychosis to March 2018, mostly of hospital patients and without appraisal of study quality, 27 studies reported the share of participants still psychotic more than a month after stopping use: the median study reported 25%, ranging from none in six laboratory studies in which volunteers were given the drug (symptoms resolved within 12 hours to 7 days) to 96%, with a median of 40% in longitudinal studies; Japanese studies reported more persistence (median 44%) than studies elsewhere (12%), which the review's authors attribute to the ICD rule allowing psychosis to last up to 6 months before a primary psychotic disorder is diagnosed, although only about a third of the Japanese studies (35%, against 6% elsewhere) used ICD-10. Second-hand reports of hospital series add 27% and 17% still psychotic beyond one and three months despite abstinence and antipsychotic treatment in 104 Japanese inpatients (cited by the systematic review); 16% and 17% after 1 and 3 months of abstinence in two reports from one Taiwanese research group, probably on one sample (a systematic review combines them as one study population of 445), with the denominator not explained and conflicting statements on family history in the narrative review that quotes them; and 10–28% beyond 6 months (narrative reviews). A 2020 meta-analysis of cohorts of substance-induced psychosis (searches 1980 to 2018, English only) pooled five estimates for amphetamine-type psychoses, 2,284 people: 22% (95% CI 14% to 34%) later received a diagnosis of schizophrenia, with extreme heterogeneity between studies (I² 96%); the five studies are not named in the article, and its methods group cocaine with methamphetamine and amphetamine as stimulants. Across all substance-induced psychoses the pooled figure was 25% (18% to 35%; 25 studies, I² 99%), highest after cannabis (34%) and lowest after alcohol (9%), and no study feature tested, including length and completeness of follow-up, significantly predicted it. Single-study figures range from 5% (China, second-hand) to about 39% in a Thai cohort of 1,116 people with methamphetamine psychosis after a first hospitalization, which four reviews report four ways: 38.8% at 5 years, nearly 40% within 6 years, 33–38% after 6–7 years together with a small cohort of 28 people, and, in the meta-analysis, 39% after 5 years with only 40% of the cohort followed up. The 2019 systematic review gives 16% within 16 years for a Finnish register study of 825 people, a narrative review gives 19–30% for register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis, and in a 24-month randomized treatment trial in Hong Kong 7 of 137 people (5.1%) with stimulant-induced psychosis and no earlier diagnosis were newly diagnosed with schizophrenia. These figures cannot show whether methamphetamine caused a lasting illness or revealed an existing vulnerability, whether some first episodes were primary psychoses attributed to drug use, or whether some later diagnoses relabel a persistent methamphetamine psychosis, since one review notes that diagnostic rules call for a primary psychotic diagnosis once psychosis persists. Recurrence with renewed use is common in clinical series, and in one follow-up positive symptoms rose in former patients who resumed use; Japanese researchers, as one review reports, describe spontaneous relapses after remission, which stressful situations seem to trigger in susceptible people. None of the single-study figures has been checked in the primary studies.
expect.magnitude: Systematic review, 27 studies with duration data: median 25% still psychotic beyond one month (laboratory studies 0%; longitudinal studies median 40%, range 14–96%; Japanese studies median 44%, range 18–96%, against 12%, range 0–39%, elsewhere; t = 4.79, p = .0001); case reports 2 of 24. Later schizophrenia diagnosis, meta-analysis (searches to 2018): amphetamines 22% (95% CI 14–34%), 5 estimates, 2284 people, I² 96%; all substance-induced psychoses 25% (18–35%), 25 studies, 34,224 people, I² 99%; cannabis 34% (25–46%); alcohol 9% (6–15%); no significant moderator. Systematic review: 33–38% after 6–7 years (two studies, 1116 and 28 people; the meta-analysis lists the Thai cohort as 39% after 5 years with 40% followed up); 16% within 16 years (825 people). Randomized treatment trial, Hong Kong: 7 of 137 (5.1%) within 24 months. Second-hand in narrative reviews: 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months (one research group, probably one sample); beyond 6 months 10–28%; later schizophrenia 5.0% (China) to 38.8% at 5 years (Thailand; nearly 40% within 6 years in another review); 19.1–30% in register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis. Japanese inpatient series cited by the systematic review: 27% beyond one month, 17% beyond three months (n=104). No pooled estimate or interval for persistence.
expect.grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim (base rates of persistence and of later diagnosis); observational, starts low. The claim rests on a systematic review read in full (Voce et al., 2019; AMSTAR 2 critically low), which reports persistence and transition figures second-hand from primary studies it did not appraise, as unweighted medians without intervals, and now also on a meta-analysis of transition read in full (Murrie et al., 2020; AMSTAR 2 low confidence, provisional, on the first reading), which pools five estimates for amphetamine-type psychoses (22%, 14% to 34%) but does not name the studies and groups cocaine with methamphetamine and amphetamine as stimulants. Risk of bias −1: mostly hospital samples, abstinence not verified, antipsychotic treatment and polydrug use not accounted for, a persistence median that includes six laboratory studies of volunteers given the drug, which observed no persistence (symptoms resolved within 12 hours to 7 days), and transition figures from register or routine diagnoses with follow-up as incomplete as 40% (the Thai cohort). Inconsistency −1: persistence ranges from 0% to 96% across studies, which the review's authors attribute to diagnostic rules (median 44% in Japanese studies against 12% elsewhere), although only 35% of the Japanese studies used ICD-10 (25% DSM-IV; elsewhere 6% and 42%), so the explanation covers about a third of them at most and is untested; the pooled transition estimate for amphetamines carries an I² of 96%, unexplained by any moderator the meta-analysis tested, single studies range from 5% to about 39%, and the Thai cohort is reported four ways by four reviews. Indirectness not downgraded: the persistence figures concern methamphetamine; the pooled transition figure covers amphetamine-type psychoses and may include some cocaine psychoses, which the statement says. Imprecision not downgraded: the pooled interval (14% to 34%) is wide, but the claim describes a range. Very low. Status mixed: persistence beyond a month ranges from 0% to 96%, and the review's partial explanations (laboratory against clinical designs; Japanese against other studies) leave a wide unexplained spread within groups (18–96% in Japan, 0–39% elsewhere); later schizophrenia diagnoses run from 5% to about 39% in single studies, with a pooled 22% and I² 96%. The inconsistency is in size, not in whether persistence or later diagnosis occurs in clinical samples. The meta-analysis and the systematic review share at least three studies (the Thai cohort, a small prospective amphetamine cohort and the Finnish register study), so they are not independent. The 5.1% within 24 months comes from a treated trial sample that included cocaine-induced psychosis and excluded, after the fact, 28 people with an earlier diagnosis. Not yet read: the register cohorts the currency check of 2026-10-16 lists.
expect.plain: Across 27 studies of meth-related psychosis, mostly in hospital patients, the typical study found 1 in 4 people still had symptoms over a month after stopping; studies ranged from none to almost all. A 2020 review found that about 1 in 5 people with amphetamine-type psychosis were later diagnosed with schizophrenia, with figures varying widely between studies; this does not show meth caused it. Psychosis often returns with renewed use.

set.plain: Across 27 studies of meth-related psychosis, mostly in hospital patients, the typical study found 1 in 4 people still had symptoms over a month after stopping; studies ranged from none to almost all. Later diagnoses of schizophrenia varied from about 1 in 20 to about 2 in 5 between studies; a 2020 review that averaged five widely differing studies of amphetamine-type psychosis found about 1 in 5. This does not show meth caused it. Psychosis often returns with renewed use.

expect.statement: In observational studies, mostly cross-sectional and mostly in treatment, psychiatric, emergency or criminal-justice samples in which the comparison group often also used other drugs, people with an amphetamine use disorder (amphetamine or methamphetamine) had higher odds of psychosis than people without one: odds ratio 2.4 (95% CI 1.6–3.5; 4 studies, I² 35%) in studies that adjusted for some combination of demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk. The review grades this estimate at its lowest level of evidence (cross-sectional associations within samples of people who use drugs); its four studies were of young offenders, people in methamphetamine rehabilitation, people using methamphetamine at least monthly, and people released from prison (a cohort): in two of them everyone used methamphetamine, so the comparison was with methamphetamine use without a use disorder, and for the prison cohort the review reports no significant relation with later primary psychosis (later substance-induced psychosis was raised). Unadjusted estimates were 3.0 (1.9–4.8; 13 studies, I² 90%) for use disorder and 2.0 (1.3–3.3; 7 studies, I² 80%) for any use; the review's authors consider unadjusted estimates likely inflated by co-occurring risk factors, and comparisons made within samples of people who use other drugs likely to understate the difference from the general population. In post hoc subgroups the association was stronger for psychotic symptoms than for diagnosed psychotic disorders; for any use, the association with a diagnosed disorder was not statistically clear (1.3, 1.0–1.9). Most studies cannot show whether use preceded psychosis. In a general-population birth cohort in Christchurch, New Zealand (962 to 1,025 people at each of five interviews from age 18 to 35), use of methamphetamine or other amphetamine-type stimulants since the previous interview went with reporting at least one psychotic symptom at the same interview (symptoms over the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25, since the previous interview at 30 and 35): odds ratio 1.88 (95% CI 1.55–2.30) unadjusted and 1.33 (1.03–1.72) after adjustment for childhood, family and adolescent factors and for concurrent cannabis use, alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and life stress; the outcome was self-reported psychotic experiences on checklist and interview items (35–42% of the cohort reported at least one in each period to age 25), not diagnosed psychosis, and use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews, so this cohort cannot show which came first either. The higher odds were concentrated in the 5% who had ever used at least weekly (2.85, 1.21–6.69, adjusted for childhood, family and adolescent factors only, not for concurrent cannabis use; about 1.3 and not statistically significant for less frequent use). No threshold level of use could be estimated; more frequent use went with more psychotic symptoms in 4 of the 8 study populations that examined it; the systematic review that counted them judged the studies finding this to be of higher quality and rated the evidence on frequency moderate, the only risk factor it rated above low. A registry cohort in Taiwan (2007–2016) followed 74,601 adults from their first arrest for using an amphetamine-type substance (urine-confirmed; the 23 substances counted include MDMA and others besides methamphetamine, with no breakdown by substance) and 298,404 insured adults of the same age, sex and index year with no record of illicit drug use, after excluding people with a psychosis diagnosis recorded before the index date: a first psychosis diagnosis was recorded at 4.68 against 0.77 per 1,000 person-years (cumulative incidence over 10 years 3.75% against 0.63%; hazard ratio 5.28, 95% CI 4.90–5.70). This orders the first arrest before the first recorded diagnosis, not the start of use before the onset of symptoms. The hazard ratio is adjusted only for age, sex and five diagnoses (depression, anxiety and three cardiovascular conditions) recorded at any time during the study, including after the arrest; other drug and alcohol use, socio-economic position and family history were not measured; the listed outcome codes omit the drug-induced psychosis codes that the text says were included; and the authors describe the analysis as exploratory and not preregistered. The hazard ratios rose with the number of arrests (4.49 for one, 6.25 for five or more), but arrests were counted over the whole follow-up and reflect police contact rather than amount of use.
expect.magnitude: Use disorder, adjusted: OR 2.4 (1.6–3.5), 4 studies, n=7648, I² 35%. Unadjusted: use disorder 3.0 (1.9–4.8), 13 studies, n=81,316, I² 90%; any use 2.0 (1.3–3.3), 7 studies, n=3436, I² 80%. Post hoc subgroups (use disorder): psychotic symptoms 4.3 (2.9–6.5) vs diagnosed disorder 2.3 (1.2–4.7). No absolute risks reported. General-population birth cohort (New Zealand): any use since the previous interview, symptoms at the same interview, OR 1.33 (1.03–1.72) after adjustment for fixed and time-varying factors (unadjusted 1.88, 1.55–2.30); ever at least weekly use 2.85 (1.21–6.69), adjusted for fixed factors only; population attributable fraction 8.0% (2.2–14.7%) if causal. Taiwan registry cohort (first arrest for an amphetamine-type substance vs no record of illicit drug use): first recorded psychosis diagnosis 4.68 vs 0.77 per 1,000 person-years; 10-year cumulative incidence 3.75% vs 0.63%; HR 5.28 (4.90–5.70) adjusted for age, sex and five comorbidity diagnoses only (crude 6.08, 5.64–6.55); by number of arrests 4.49 (one) to 6.25 (five or more).
expect.plain: In studies mostly in treatment, hospitals or prisons, a meth or amphetamine use disorder went with about two and a half times the odds of psychosis, allowing for some other differences. A study following about 1,000 New Zealanders from birth found any use went with slightly more self-reported psychotic experiences, mostly in people who had ever used at least weekly. In Taiwan, about 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs were diagnosed with psychosis within 10 years, against under 1 in 100 people with no drug record; few other differences were allowed for. None of these studies settles which came first.
expect.grade.reasoning: Observational, mostly cross-sectional; starts low. The claim is an association and rests on the adjusted use-disorder estimate (2.4, 1.6–3.5; 4 studies, I² 35%); the unadjusted estimates are context, labelled as likely inflated. Risk of bias not downgraded: the adjusted studies accounted for some combination of demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk, the adjusted pool's weighted quality score is 88% in the review, and comparison groups mostly also used other drugs (in two of the four adjusted studies, methamphetamine without a use disorder), which the authors argue makes estimates understate the difference from the general population; residual confounding by unmeasured premorbid factors (family history of psychosis, childhood trauma) remains and is why the claim is worded as an association. Inconsistency not downgraded for the adjusted estimate; the unadjusted estimates are heterogeneous (I² 80–90%). Publication bias could not be assessed (too few studies; AMSTAR 2 critically low); not downgraded, noted. Not upgraded for dose–response: frequency was associated in 4 of 8 populations (evidence the risk-factor review rates moderate), but across different studies and measures rather than as a gradient within one body of evidence; the within-person gradient is rated in the claim on frequency of use within the same people (section 9). McKetin et al. (2013), rated separately in that claim, is inside the unadjusted any-use estimate and is the review's only adjusted any-use estimate (5.3); it is not in the adjusted use-disorder estimate on which this claim rests. Boden et al. (2023), a general-population birth cohort read in full (ROBINS-E high on the first reading, from concerns in several domains), agrees in direction and is smaller after fuller adjustment (any use, OR 1.33, 1.03–1.72, after adjusting for concurrent cannabis use and other time-varying factors; 1.88 unadjusted), which fits the meta-analysis authors' view that unadjusted estimates are inflated; it is not counted as inconsistency, because exposure (any use rather than use disorder), population and outcome (self-reported psychotic experiences) differ. Not upgraded for dose–response: its gradient (2.85 for ever at least weekly use against about 1.3, not significant, for less frequent use) is adjusted only for fixed confounders, is not monotonic (1.37, 1.32, 2.85) and rests on 51 people in the top category. It is an independent sample, though it shares an author with McKetin et al. (2013) and the meta-analysis. Huang et al. (2022), a Taiwanese registry cohort read in full (ROBINS-E very high on its first-pass card, from confounding), agrees in direction with a much larger estimate (HR 5.28, 4.90–5.70) for a first recorded psychosis diagnosis after a first arrest for an amphetamine-type substance, against insured people with no drug record. It is not counted as inconsistency, because exposure (arrest, with MDMA and other substances pooled with methamphetamine), comparator (no record of any illicit drug use) and outcome (claims diagnoses) differ and the adjustment is minimal: age, sex and five comorbidity codes partly recorded after the arrest, nothing for other drug or alcohol use, socio-economic position or family history. It does not earn an upgrade for large effect, because these remaining biases, and more contact with services after arrest, all run away from the null; nor for dose–response, because its gradient by number of arrests uses arrests counted over the whole follow-up (more arrests go with longer observation) and its printed trend test is reproduced by a regression on five category rates. Its rehabilitation comparison (HR 0.74 for the roughly 10% offered treatment under deferred prosecution, chosen by prosecutors for promising outcomes) is not used. It is an independent sample from a different country and design, so it adds to the replication of the direction, not to the precision of any one estimate.

expect.statement: Among US adults aged 18–64, estimated past-year methamphetamine use rose from about 1.61 million in 2015 to 1.97 million in 2019 (about +22%, editors' calculation) and past-year methamphetamine use disorder (DSM-IV criteria) from about 741,000 to 1.09 million (about +47%, editors' calculation), while overdose deaths involving psychostimulants other than cocaine rose from 5,526 to 15,489 (+180%). More than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths not involving opioids also rose, from 3,220 to 7,051. The death code (ICD-10 T43.6) covers psychostimulants other than cocaine; the authors report that about 85–90% of such certificates mention methamphetamine. The survey excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people and relies on self-report, so use is probably underestimated. The paper's headline increases for use (43%) and for use disorder without injection (105%) are calculated from 2016, the lowest year, not from 2015. These 2015–2019 figures (ages 18–64, DSM-IV) are not comparable with the 2024 survey figures shown in this section (ages 12 and over, DSM-5). Counting all ages, overdose deaths that a later analysis of the national death records labels methamphetamine-involved (its ICD-10 codes are given only in a supplement, not read) rose from 547 in 1999 to 34,855 in 2023 (crude rate 0.20 to 10.41 per 100,000; 2023 data provisional). The increase averaged 18.5% a year, was steepest in 2018–2021 (37.4% a year) and slowed to 3.4% a year (95% CI 0.2–6.8) in 2021–2023. Deaths involving methamphetamine with fentanyl rose by 76% a year in 2012–2021 and 8.6% a year in 2021–2023, while those with other opioids fell by 27% a year in 2021–2023; no count or share of methamphetamine-involved deaths that also involved opioids is printed (a figure plots their rates, and the overlap of the fentanyl and other-opioid series is not given). The analysis gives two counts for 2023 (34,855 and 35,126), its rates are crude rather than age-adjusted, and its all-ages series is not directly comparable with the 2015–2019 counts for ages 18–64. A CDC report gives the same 2023 count (34,855), citing a national statistics brief, for deaths with the code for psychostimulants other than cocaine (T43.6), which suggests that the later analysis used that code (editors' inference); on that code, the age-adjusted death rate rose from 3.9 per 100,000 in 2018 to 10.4 in 2023, and the report says the largest increases were in deaths that also involved opioids, without giving those figures. The same report draws on a CDC surveillance system that names methamphetamine from medical examiner, coroner and toxicology reports (49 states and the District of Columbia, four of them for only part of the period, pooled over January 2021 to June 2024): methamphetamine was involved in 96,614 of 309,274 overdose deaths (31.2%); 68.8% of these also involved opioids and 30,139 (9.7% of all overdose deaths) did not. This share comes from a different system and period than the 2019 share above, so the two are not directly comparable. Decedents without opioids were older (64% aged 45 or over, against 39% of those with opioids; editors' calculation) and more often had a recorded history of cardiovascular disease (39.3% against 19.8%). The report's authors expect stimulant-involved deaths to be undercounted, because some are certified as cardiovascular deaths without an overdose code and toxicology testing varies.
expect.plain: In US household surveys of adults aged 18 to 64, the estimated number who said they had used meth in the past year rose by about a fifth between 2015 and 2019, and the number with a meth use disorder by about half; the surveys miss people who are homeless or in institutions. Over the same years, overdose deaths involving stimulants other than cocaine (mostly meth) nearly tripled; more than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths without opioids also more than doubled. The bigger percentages often quoted from this paper start from 2016, the lowest year. Later US survey figures use different methods and are not directly comparable. Newer death records for all ages show that deaths involving meth kept rising, from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023, but the rise slowed after 2021 (the latest year's figures are provisional). Deaths involving both meth and fentanyl rose fastest. These newer counts come from the same death records and include all ages, so they extend the earlier figures rather than confirm them. A CDC report that used medical examiners' and toxicology reports found meth in about 31 in 100 overdose deaths from 2021 to mid-2024; about 7 in 10 of those deaths also involved opioids, and about 3 in 10 did not.
expect.grade.reasoning: Repeated national survey (NSDUH) and death-certificate counts; observational, starts low (§6.3). Not upgraded: large effect concerns the size of an exposure's effect under adjustment, not a change in counts over time (§6.3, descriptive claims), and the survey trends (+22% use, +47% use disorder; intervals overlapping between 2015 and 2019; trend tests significant) are not large. Risk of bias not downgraded for the trend (JBI moderate): the frame excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people and about half of sampled people completed an interview, which lowers the levels more than it changes the trend. The death series is a code (ICD-10 T43.6), about 85–90% of whose certificates mention methamphetamine, and about 6% of 2019 overdose certificates named no drug, so the counts are a proxy and an undercount. The all-ages extension to 2023 (Zhu et al., 2025; JBI moderate on its study card) draws on the same national death records, so it extends the series rather than replicating it (status stays single-study); its codes are not shown in the article, 2023 data are provisional, two different 2023 counts are given and two subgroup averages in its table appear transposed. These faults affect exact figures, not the direction of the rise or the timing of the slowdown after 2021, so the rating is not downgraded; the 2021–2023 slowdown is a segment fitted to three yearly values, the last of them provisional. The CDC report (Tanz et al., 2025; JBI moderate on its first-pass card), read in full, uses the same national death records for its 2018–2023 rates, so it too extends rather than replicates the series (status stays single-study); its 2023 count matches the later analysis, which suggests that both use the T43.6 code. Its SUDORS figures come from a partly separate source (medical examiner, coroner and toxicology reports naming methamphetamine) and give the opioid share that the death-code analyses lacked, but they are pooled over one period, cover four states for only part of it, and cannot show a trend. The authors expect an undercount; in the editors' reading it may fall more on deaths without opioids (deaths certified as cardiovascular are the ones missed, and decedents without opioids were older and more often had cardiovascular disease), so the share with opioids may be somewhat overstated. Not downgraded: these limits affect exact shares, not the order of magnitude.

expect.statement: In the studies that compared group means with population norms, average test scores of people with methamphetamine dependence mostly fell in the low-average to average range: between the 16th and 55th percentiles after about 6 days of verified abstinence in one study, whose authors set the impaired range at the 2nd percentile or below. A group mean in the normal range does not show that every individual is, nor does it exclude a decline from a higher starting point. No study tested people before they began to use. One study from the same laboratory as the percentile study (Dean et al., 2018; 37 people with methamphetamine dependence after about a week of abstinence, 41 controls) predicted each person's adult score from school grades before first use, parental income, age and smoking, with a model fitted in the controls that explained about 40% of their variance: the methamphetamine group's grades before first use were already lower (grade point average 2.1 against 2.5), and their adult scores fell below the prediction (overall, a standardized paired difference of 0.61; attention 0.69, memory 0.46; executive function not below). These scores were standardized to the controls, not to population norms, the model's own uncertainty was not carried into the tests, and other substance use disorders were far more common in the methamphetamine group. One review disputes reading normed scores as a categorical line, arguing that mild deficits can still matter, and cites initial evidence of lower scores on performance measures of everyday functioning (Dean et al., 2013). A minority met impairment criteria, more often than controls: about 7 of 27 people who used methamphetamine versus 2 of 18 controls met a 2-SD criterion in at least one domain in one study (as summarized, with ambiguous wording, in a review; for working memory alone, 1 versus 2; the primary paper is still to be read), and 34% of the methamphetamine group versus 16% of controls had a global deficit score above 0.5 in another (a cut-off the authors equate with roughly the 16th percentile and describe as relatively liberal, though validated and widely used), in which only the group that kept using differed significantly (38%; abstainers 24%), more than half of the methamphetamine group but no controls had HIV, and controls were also screened free of hepatitis C, ADHD and antisocial personality disorder.
expect.magnitude: Group means between about the 16th and 55th percentiles on normed tests (Simon et al., 2010); impaired in at least one domain 7/27 (26%) vs 2/18 (11%) (Kalechstein et al., 2003, as reported by Hart et al., 2012); globally impaired 34% vs 16% (Iudicello et al., 2010). Against a prediction from pre-use school grades, parental income, age and smoking (Dean et al., 2018; 37 vs 41): overall d 0.61 (paired t(36) 3.73, p = 0.001), attention 0.69, memory 0.46, executive function not below; pre-use grade point average 2.1 vs 2.5 (p = 0.016).
expect.plain: In the studies that compared them with test norms, groups of people dependent on meth scored on average in the low-average to average range, not in the range the authors called impaired. An average in the normal range does not mean every person is, and it cannot show whether someone's scores dropped from a higher starting point. No one was tested before they started using meth. One study used school grades from before first use to estimate how well people should do as adults: people dependent on meth scored lower than expected, mostly on attention and memory tests, but their school grades had already been lower than the comparison group's, and they were tested only about a week after stopping. One review argues that even a small drop within the normal range can matter, pointing to early evidence of lower scores on tests of everyday tasks. In two studies that counted individuals, about a quarter to a third of people who used meth met a definition of impairment, compared with about one in nine to one in six people who didn't. The two studies drew the line differently: one counted very low scores (about the bottom 2%) in any one area, the other an overall score in roughly the bottom sixth. In one of them, more than half of the people who used meth had HIV and none of the comparison group did, which could explain part of that difference.
expect.grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low. Risk of bias: different impairment definitions and norm sets; group means compared with norms without demographic matching; in the impairment-rate study, HIV, hepatitis C, ADHD and antisocial personality disorder present only in people who used methamphetamine. Imprecision: the proportions come from samples of 27 vs 18 and 83 vs 38. Status replicated for group means; the higher impairment rate in people who used methamphetamine rests on two studies, one reported second-hand and one confounded by HIV. Dean et al. (2018; ROBINS-E high on its first-pass card), from the same laboratory as Simon et al. (2010) and the review by Dean et al. (2013), qualifies the caveat that no starting point was measured: it estimates one from school grades before first use, a proxy rather than a pre-use test, with a prediction model fitted in 41 controls that explains about 40% of the variance and whose uncertainty the paired tests ignore, scores standardized to the controls rather than to norms, testing after about a week of abstinence, and far more other substance use disorders in the methamphetamine group. It bears on whether scores fell from a higher starting point, not on whether group means lie within norms, so it changes neither the rating nor the status.
